text:
Yes. There is such a thing as a duty to oneself, and a person can do wrong even when the direct harm falls only on themselves.

The strongest reason is that morality is not only about how we treat other people; it is also about how we treat rational agency, dignity, and human life—including our own. If I matter morally, then I cannot be morally irrelevant just because I am the one being harmed. To say “it’s only me” assumes that the self has no claim to respect. But that is false. A person is not a disposable object merely because they own that object. They are a being with value, and that value imposes limits on what they may do to themselves.

One way to put this is in Kantian terms: each person has a duty to respect humanity, both in others and in themselves. If I lie to another person, I wrong them by using them merely as a means. But if I degrade, destroy, or recklessly damage myself for trivial reasons, I also fail to respect humanity in my own person. I treat my rational capacities, health, or life as expendable. That is morally significant even if no one else is directly injured.

Consider some examples. Suppose someone knowingly ruins their mind with an addictive substance, not from desperation or illness, but from indifference to their own future agency. Or suppose someone humiliates themselves for money in a way that corrodes their self-respect and character. Or suppose someone attempts suicide not in a case of unbearable terminal suffering, but from a cultivated contempt for their own worth. In each case, our moral criticism is not exhausted by concern for third parties. We think something bad has happened to the person’s relation to themselves. They have betrayed, neglected, or violated something they owe to themselves.

An opponent might say: wrongness requires a victim distinct from the actor. If I choose badly for myself, that may be foolish or imprudent, but not immoral. This view has some appeal because morality often concerns interpersonal duties like honesty, fairness, and nonviolence. But it is too narrow. It cannot easily explain why self-enslavement, self-mutilation for amusement, or the deliberate destruction of one’s own basic capacities often strike us as more than mere mistakes. Prudence says, “this will go badly for you.” Morality says, “you should not treat a person that way”—and that person can be yourself.

There is also a deeper problem with denying duties to oneself. If persons have intrinsic worth, that worth should not disappear when the person and the agent are identical. Otherwise, morality would bizarrely imply: “Everyone must respect you—except you.” That is backwards. In many ways, you are the first person responsible for honoring your own dignity.

That said, duties to oneself should be used carefully. They can become excuses for paternalism, moralism, or cruelty toward people who are suffering. Not every unhealthy choice is a moral failure. People act under addiction, depression, ignorance, trauma, and constraint. We should distinguish sin from sickness, vice from pain, and serious self-violation from ordinary imperfection. A duty to oneself does not mean one must optimize one’s life at every moment or that strangers may police every personal choice.

Still, the core point remains: a person can wrong themselves. They do so when they needlessly damage or debase the very capacities and dignity that make them a moral being. Having no dependents does not erase that fact. It only removes one class of reasons against the action. It does not remove all of them.

So my position is: yes, there is a duty to oneself, and yes, someone who harms only themselves can still do something morally wrong.
